title: Drake Sued Over “Janice STFU” Claim: Songwriter Says Chorus Is Identical to His Demo
body:
The rapper’s latest chart‑topping single, “Janice STFU,” has been thrust into the courtroom after a Los Angeles‑based songwriter filed a lawsuit alleging that Drake’s hook was lifted directly from an unpublished demo. The plaintiff, whose identity is being protected for now, claims the chorus of the track is “literally identical” to a melody and lyric structure he submitted to a music publishing firm in early 2023, only to see it reappear on Drake’s October release without any credit or compensation.

According to the complaint, the songwriter—who has been working in the industry as a co‑writer and vocal producer for several years—first shared his demo, titled “Janice,” with a third‑party publishing company that later facilitated a meeting with Drake’s team. The document allegedly contains the same three‑note vocal motif and the recurring “STFU” refrain that forms the backbone of Drake’s hook. The filing asserts that after the demo was presented, Drake’s camp recorded a version of the song, altered the verses, and released it as part of his “Iceman” album, which has already amassed millions of streams worldwide.

Legal experts note that claims of melodic similarity are common in the music business, but proving infringement hinges on demonstrating that the accused had access to the original work and that the two pieces are substantially similar. “The plaintiff’s strongest argument is the alleged chain of custody through the publishing intermediary,” said entertainment attorney Maya Patel of the law firm Green & Harlow. “If they can establish that Drake’s producers received the demo and that the hook is not a generic phrase or a common melodic contour, the case could have merit.” Patel added that the “STFU” chant, while colloquial, may be deemed a distinctive lyrical element if it appears in the same rhythmic and melodic context.

Drake’s legal team has not publicly responded to the filing, but they have a history of settling disputes out of court. In 2020, the artist’s representatives reached a confidential agreement with a songwriter who claimed a similar breach of rights on a different track. Industry insiders suggest that the current lawsuit could follow a comparable path, especially given the high stakes of a single that is already generating substantial revenue through streaming, radio play, and sync licenses. “The financial exposure is significant,” said music‑industry analyst Carlos Mendez. “Even a modest settlement could run into the low six figures, not to mention the potential reputational damage if the case proceeds to trial.”

The dispute also shines a light on the broader conversation about how major artists source material in the era of digital collaboration. With a network of producers, beat‑makers, and songwriters contributing to a single project, the lines between inspiration, sampling, and outright copying can become blurred. Critics argue that high‑profile musicians benefit from a system that often leaves lesser‑known creators without proper acknowledgment. Advocacy groups have called for more transparent crediting practices and stronger contractual safeguards to protect songwriters’ intellectual property.

As the lawsuit moves forward, both parties will likely engage in discovery to verify the timeline of the demo’s circulation and the creative process behind “Janice STFU.” The court’s decision could set a precedent for how similar claims are evaluated in the streaming age, where songs can achieve global success within days of release. For now, fans await further developments while the track continues to dominate playlists, and the music‑industry community watches closely to see whether the alleged infringement will reshape the standards of collaboration and credit in popular music.
